<!-- Generated by R/build_report.R from report/README.Rmd. Edit the .Rmd, not this file. -->

PaleoACES compares climate-predicted and observed forest composition in Mount Rainier (MORA) and
North Cascades (NOCA) National Parks, using forest resurveys and four Holocene macrofossil records.
One CCA calibrated on the legacy survey plots provides the shared coordinate system.

This page is the supplementary appendix of the analysis. It shows every main and supplementary
figure, the tables reported in the manuscript and the modelling code, in the order of the analysis
and of the Supporting Information (Appendix S1, Appendix S2). Data cleaning is summarized by its
figure here; the step-by-step detail sits in [`report/details/`](report/details), linked from
each section.

```sh
Rscript R/run_all.R --offline   # run the whole analysis from the cached climate (add --age-models to refit Bacon)
Rscript R/build_report.R        # rebuild this page and report/ from the outputs
```

# The remodelled analysis at a glance

The Holocene side of the analysis is being remodelled on lake-periods: one lake within one climate
period, compared from its first to its last sampled century. Each row below is filled when its step
is finished.

| Step | What it does | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Step 0 | Climate variables and CCA refit | `r sprintf('MSpT + SP: VIF %.2f, adjusted R² %.3f (all four %.3f), no lake-century outside the calibration climate, display rotation %.1f°', max(read_output("cca_screening.csv")$VIF[read_output("cca_screening.csv")$set == "MSpT + SP"]), read_output("cca_screening.csv")$adjusted_R2[read_output("cca_screening.csv")$set == "MSpT + SP"][1], read_output("cca_screening.csv")$adjusted_R2[1], read_output("cca_display_rotation.csv")$angle_degrees)` |
| Step 1 | Climate periods and lake-periods | `r p = read_output('holocene_periods.csv'); sprintf('%d periods from %d to %d cal BP (%d C, %d S), none split', nrow(p), max(p$older_cal_bp), min(p$younger_cal_bp), sum(p$period_type == "Holocene-C"), sum(p$period_type == "Holocene-S"))` |
| Steps 2 to 4 | Mismatch, lag, turnover, pace, direction, climate change rate and fire per lake-period | `r u = read_output('cca_tracking_lake_periods.csv'); sprintf('%d lake-periods (MORA %d, NOCA %d, %d C, %d S), %d to %d years long', nrow(u), sum(u$site == "MORA"), sum(u$site == "NOCA"), sum(u$period_type == "Holocene-C"), sum(u$period_type == "Holocene-S"), min(u$duration_yr), max(u$duration_yr))` |
| Step 5 | Holocene explanatory models | `r x = read_output('community_predictor_models/model_coefficients.csv') |> dplyr::filter(era == 'Holocene'); g = function(m, t) x[x$metric == m & x$term == t, ]; sprintf('Lag rate rises with climate change rate (%+.2f, %.2f to %.2f), fire goes with a larger direction effect (%+.2f, %.2f to %.2f)', g('lag_rate','climate_rate')$estimate, g('lag_rate','climate_rate')$conf_low, g('lag_rate','climate_rate')$conf_high, g('direction_effect','fire_activity')$estimate, g('direction_effect','fire_activity')$conf_low, g('direction_effect','fire_activity')$conf_high)` |
| Step 5a | Holocene against Anthropocene (era models) | `r f = read_output('era_comparison/era_folds.csv'); g = function(r, p) f$fold[f$response == r & f$site == p & f$against == 'Holocene-C']; sprintf('Anthropocene climate change %.0f (MORA) and %.0f (NOCA) times faster than in Holocene-C periods, turnover %.0f and %.0f times faster', g('climate_rate','MORA'), g('climate_rate','NOCA'), g('turnover_rate','MORA'), g('turnover_rate','NOCA'))` |
| Step 6 | Species contributions | `r m = read_output('species_contribution_models/species_means.csv'); h = m[m$period_type != 'Anthropocene' & m$interval_defined, ]; a = m[m$period_type == 'Anthropocene' & m$interval_defined & m$measure == 'contrib_lag', ]; sprintf('Holocene species means near zero (%d of %d intervals span zero). Anthropocene lag rate split into species and climate: %d of %d species-park means narrow the lag, %d widen it', sum(h$conf_low <= 0 & h$conf_high >= 0), nrow(h), sum(a$conf_high < 0), nrow(a), sum(a$conf_low > 0))` |

# Step 0. Climate variables and the CCA

**What and why.** The four seasonal variables come in two tightly linked pairs: spring and winter
temperature, and summer and winter precipitation. Inside a pair the CCA cannot tell the two
seasons apart, and Holocene lakes reach seasonal combinations the modern plots never show. The CCA
is therefore constrained by one variable of each pair. Spring temperature (MSpT) stands for
snowmelt timing and the start of the growing season. Summer precipitation (SP) stands for summer
drying stress. Because each pair is strongly correlated, the two also carry temperature and
precipitation change in general.

**How it is calculated.**

```{r step0-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/10_cca.R', 'cca-fit')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/10_cca.R', 'cca-projection')
```

**Result.**

```{r step0-screening}
screening = read_output('cca_screening.csv')
screening |> group_by(set) |> summarise(Variables = gsub(';', ', ', first(variables)),
    `Largest abs. correlation` = first(max_abs_correlation),
    `VIF` = paste(sprintf('%s %.1f', variable, VIF), collapse = ', '),
    `R²` = first(R2), `Adjusted R²` = first(adjusted_R2),
    `MORA lake-centuries outside (%)` = 100 * first(extrapolated_share_MORA),
    `NOCA lake-centuries outside (%)` = 100 * first(extrapolated_share_NOCA), .groups = 'drop') |>
  arrange(match(set, c('All four', 'MWT + SP', 'MSpT + SP'))) |> rename(Set = set) |>
  show_table('step0_screening', caption = sprintf(paste('**Screening of the climate constraints** on the %d',
    'legacy calibration plots. Holocene lake-centuries: %d at MORA (three lakes) and %d at NOCA.'),
    screening$n_plots[1], screening$holocene_lake_centuries_MORA[1], screening$holocene_lake_centuries_NOCA[1]))
addback = read_output('cca_screening_addback.csv')
rotation = read_output('cca_display_rotation.csv')
```

With MSpT and SP the CCA explains `r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * screening$adjusted_R2[screening$set == 'MSpT + SP'][1])`
of the variation in composition (adjusted R²), against
`r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * screening$adjusted_R2[screening$set == 'All four'][1])` with all four
variables. Adding winter temperature and winter precipitation back improves the fit
(pseudo-F `r sprintf('%.2f', addback$pseudo_F[1])`, p = `r sprintf('%.4f', addback$p_value[addback$design == 'Unrestricted'])`
unrestricted and p = `r sprintf('%.4f', addback$p_value[addback$design == 'Within parks'])` within parks).
That gain comes from the seasonal contrasts within each pair, the same contrasts that make the
four-variable fit collinear (VIF up to `r sprintf('%.1f', max(screening$VIF[screening$set == 'All four']))`)
and that place `r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * screening$extrapolated_share_MORA[screening$set == 'All four'][1])`
of the MORA lake-centuries outside the calibration climate. With MSpT and SP no lake-century in
either park is outside it. The display rotation turns the plane by
`r sprintf('%.1f', rotation$angle_degrees)` degrees so that rotated axis 1 is spring temperature
increasing to the right and rotated axis 2 summer precipitation increasing upward. The pipeline
asserts that mismatch, lag, turnover, pace and direction are identical before and after this rotation.

# Step 1. Climate periods

**What and why.** The Holocene is cut into climate-change (C) periods, when the park-average
climate of the lakes moved steadily in one direction, and stability (S) periods between them. The
rules of the climate-era step are unchanged. Only their input changed: the periods are now drawn
from the two CCA variables, MSpT and SP, so that the periods describe change along the same
climate axes that the CCA uses. A climate-change period that contains a long internal trough of
low change is split into sub-periods (a, b, c). Each period, or sub-period, is one unit for the
lake-periods of the next step.

**Result.**

```{r step1-periods}
comparison = read_output('holocene_period_comparison.csv')
comparison |> transmute(Catalog = catalog, Period = period, Type = period_type,
    `Older (cal BP)` = older_cal_bp, `Younger (cal BP)` = younger_cal_bp,
    `Duration (years)` = duration_years, Drivers = gsub(';', ', ', coalesce(drivers, ''))) |>
  show_table('step1_periods', caption = paste('**Climate periods** drawn from MSpT and SP (used from',
    'Step 1 on) and, by the same rules, from all four seasonal variables (the periods before Step 0).'))
periods = comparison |> filter(startsWith(catalog, 'MSpT'))
```

With MSpT and SP the Holocene from `r max(periods$older_cal_bp)` to `r min(periods$younger_cal_bp)`
cal BP falls into `r sum(periods$period_type == 'Holocene-C')` climate-change periods and
`r sum(periods$period_type == 'Holocene-S')` stability periods, and no climate-change period is
split. The first four-variable climate-change period (C1a to C1c, 9600 to 7200 cal BP) becomes C1,
S1 and C2: its middle part (8600 to 8200 cal BP) was driven by winter wetting alone, which is no
longer a constraint. From 7200 cal BP onward every boundary is unchanged, and the periods are
renumbered. The high-fire periods do not depend on the CCA and are unchanged.

```{r fig-2-main}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_climate_levels_eras_fire.pdf')
rates2 = read_output('figures/anthropocene_climate_rates.csv')
r2 = function(v, park) { x = rates2[rates2$variable == v & rates2$site == park, ]
  if (v == 'SP') sprintf('%+.0f mm (%+.1f SD)', x$rate, x$z_rate) else sprintf('%+.2f °C (%+.1f SD)', x$rate, x$z_rate) }
```

**Figure 2. Holocene climate and fire.** (A) Spring temperature (°C) and (B) summer
precipitation (mm), the two CCA constraints, averaged over the lakes of each park with the two parks
weighted equally (CHELSA-TraCE21k). Bold lines are 1,000-year running means and thin lines the
centennial series. Shading marks the climate-change (C) and stability (S) periods, with the change
that drove each climate-change period written below its name (cooling or warming of spring temperature, drying or
wetting of summer precipitation). Labels linked to the bold lines give the change per century over a period for each
variable that drove it. A cross marks the largest step between two consecutive centuries, labelled with its rate. To the right of each panel, the Anthropocene change per century from
the legacy to the resurvey climate window, the median over plots in each park: spring temperature
`r sprintf('%+.2f', rates2$rate[rates2$variable == 'MSpT' & rates2$site == 'MORA'])` °C at MORA and
`r sprintf('%+.2f', rates2$rate[rates2$variable == 'MSpT' & rates2$site == 'NOCA'])` °C at NOCA, summer precipitation
`r sprintf('%+.1f', rates2$rate[rates2$variable == 'SP' & rates2$site == 'MORA'])` mm at MORA and
`r sprintf('%+.1f', rates2$rate[rates2$variable == 'SP' & rates2$site == 'NOCA'])` mm at NOCA. These come from a change
over about 29 years, while each Holocene rate spans a whole period of 400 to 2,700 years. (C) Fire-frequency
ratio of each park, the frequency of accepted fire events relative to the park's high-fire threshold.
Values above 1 (red) are high-fire periods.

# Steps 1 to 4. Lake-periods and their responses

## Positions per sampled century

**What and why.** Each macrofossil sample has an observed position in the CCA plane (its WA score,
from the taxa it contains). Each lake also has a climate-predicted position for every century
(its LC score, from that lake's own climate cell). Samples are dated by the median of their Bacon
ages and grouped by century. The observed position of a century is the centroid of its samples'
WA positions. No vegetation is interpolated between sampled centuries. These century positions
feed the lake-periods below and the period centroids of Figure 3. No model is fitted on the
century steps any more.

```{r step1-positions}
positions = read_output('cca_tracking_holocene_century_positions.csv')
positions |> group_by(Park = site, Lake = lake) |>
  summarise(`Sampled centuries` = n(), Samples = sum(n_samples),
    `Centuries with one sample` = sum(n_samples == 1),
    `Oldest (cal BP)` = max(century_cal_bp), `Youngest (cal BP)` = min(century_cal_bp), .groups = 'drop') |>
  show_table('step1_sampled_centuries', caption = '**Sampled centuries per lake** on the MSpT + SP CCA.')
```

The three MORA lakes begin about 6,850 cal BP and most of their centuries rest on a single sample.
Panther Potholes (NOCA) covers the whole Holocene with several samples per century.

Stages and helpers: [`R/pipeline/12_tracking.R`](R/pipeline/12_tracking.R),
[`R/helpers/century_tracking.R`](R/helpers/century_tracking.R),
[`R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R`](R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R).

## Lake-periods

**What and why.** Two scoops of sediment from the same forest in the same century differ by
about as much as the forest drifts in many centuries, because one needle caught or missed moves a
sample's position. A lag computed between consecutive centuries is therefore mostly that noise.
Comparing the two ends of a whole climate period lets the drift outgrow it. A lake-period is one
lake within one climate period. Its start (t1) is the oldest and its end (t2) the youngest
sampled century of that lake in that period, and a lake needs samples in at least two centuries
of a period to have a lake-period there. The centuries in between enter no model.

At each end the mismatch M is the distance between the observed and the climate-predicted
positions. The lag rate is the change in M per century. The turnover rate is the length of the
observed movement per century. The pace and direction effects ask how much smaller the final
mismatch would have been if the community had moved the predicted distance in its own direction
(pace) or its own distance in the predicted direction (direction). The climate change rate is the
standardized end-to-end change of MSpT and SP in the lake's own climate cell, per century. Fire
activity is the number of accepted fire events between t1 and t2, per century and per charcoal
core, averaged over the cores of the park that cover the whole lake-period.

**How it is calculated.** The code below computes every quantity from the two ends of a unit, a
Holocene lake-period or an Anthropocene plot pair. The comments say what each step means.

```{r step24-code}
code_snippet('R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R', 'tracking-geometry')
code_snippet('R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R', 'tracking-corrections')
```

**Result.**

```{r step24-units}
candidates = read_output('cca_tracking_lake_period_candidates.csv')
units = read_output('cca_tracking_lake_periods.csv')
units |> transmute(Park = site, Lake = lake, Period = period, `t1 (cal BP)` = age_start,
    `t2 (cal BP)` = age_end, `Years` = duration_yr, `Samples t1` = n_start, `Samples t2` = n_end,
    `Climate change rate` = climate_rate, `MSpT change (°C)` = MSpT_change, `SP change (mm)` = SP_change,
    `Fire activity` = fire_activity, `M t1` = M_start, `M t2` = M_end, `Lag rate` = lag_rate,
    `Turnover rate` = turnover_rate, `Pace effect` = pace_effect, `Direction effect` = direction_effect) |>
  show_table('step24_lake_periods', caption = paste('**Lake-periods.** Rates are per century: climate',
    'change in calibration SD, fire in events per covered core, the others in CCA distance.',
    'Pace and direction are undefined where the observed or the predicted position did not move.'))
```

Of the `r nrow(candidates)` lake and period combinations with at least one sampled century,
`r nrow(units)` have samples in two or more centuries and become lake-periods
(MORA `r sum(units$site == 'MORA')`, NOCA `r sum(units$site == 'NOCA')`,
`r sum(units$period_type == 'Holocene-C')` in climate-change and
`r sum(units$period_type == 'Holocene-S')` in stability periods). They span
`r min(units$duration_yr)` to `r max(units$duration_yr)` years. Every MORA end rests on a
single sample, and `r sum(!units$direction_defined & units$site == 'MORA')` MORA lake-periods have no defined direction
because the observed or predicted position did not move. All lake-periods have fire coverage.

# Step 5. What goes with lag rate, pace and direction in the Holocene

**What and why.** Within the Holocene lake-periods, does a period with more climate change, or
more fire, end with a larger lag, and with better or worse pace and direction? Each response is
modelled on the park, the climate change rate and fire activity together. Consecutive
lake-periods of a lake can share an end century, so their errors are related, and an AR(1) term
on the order of the lake-periods within each lake carries that from the start. Ends that rest on
a single sample are noisier, so each row is weighted by the sampling variance of its two ends,
and the parks keep different residual spread. In the Anthropocene the same responses are
compared between burned and unburned plots within each park.

**How it is calculated.**

```{r step5-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/14_predictor_models.R', 'holocene-explanatory-model')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/14_predictor_models.R', 'anthropocene-explanatory-model')
```

**Result.**

```{r step5-results}
coefficients = read_output('community_predictor_models/model_coefficients.csv')
performance = read_output('community_predictor_models/model_performance.csv')
label = c(lag_rate = 'Lag rate', pace_effect = 'Pace effect', direction_effect = 'Direction effect',
  lag = 'Lag (not divided by time)', pace_effect_total = 'Pace effect (not divided by time)',
  direction_effect_total = 'Direction effect (not divided by time)')
coefficients |> left_join(performance |> select(metric = response, era, n, R2, sd_ratio_NOCA_to_MORA, AR1_phi),
    by = c('metric', 'era')) |>
  transmute(Response = label[metric], Era = era, Term = term, Estimate = estimate,
    `95% CI` = sprintf('%.3f to %.3f', conf_low, conf_high), p = p_value, n,
    `R²` = R2, `SD ratio NOCA/MORA` = sd_ratio_NOCA_to_MORA, `AR(1)` = AR1_phi) |>
  show_table('step5_explanatory_models', caption = paste('**Explanatory models.** Holocene:',
    'response ~ site + climate_rate + fire_activity for the per-century responses and',
    'response ~ site + climate_change + fire_activity for the responses not divided by time, on the',
    'lake-periods, AR(1) within lake, endpoint weights. Anthropocene: response ~ site + burned on the plot',
    'pairs. Estimates in CCA distance (per century for the per-century responses) per unit of the term.',
    'Conditional 95% confidence intervals. R² is descriptive (1 − SSE/SST).'))
slope = function(m, t) coefficients |> filter(metric == m, era == 'Holocene', term == t)
f = function(x) sprintf('%+.2f (%.2f to %.2f)', x$estimate, x$conf_low, x$conf_high)
```

In the Holocene, lake-periods with faster climate change ended with a larger lag
(`r f(slope('lag_rate', 'climate_rate'))` CCA distance per century for one more standardized
unit of climate change per century) and with a larger pace effect
(`r f(slope('pace_effect', 'climate_rate'))`). Fire activity did not go with the lag rate
(`r f(slope('lag_rate', 'fire_activity'))` per extra event per century per core), but it went with
a larger direction effect (`r f(slope('direction_effect', 'fire_activity'))`): where fire was more
frequent, the community's direction was further from the predicted one. The fire values of the two
parks barely overlap. The site term absorbs the difference between the parks, so the fire slope
comes from the narrow range within each park
(`r u = read_output('cca_tracking_lake_periods.csv'); paste(sprintf('%s %.2f to %.2f', c('MORA', 'NOCA'), tapply(u$fire_activity, u$site, min), tapply(u$fire_activity, u$site, max)), collapse = ', ')`
events per century per core).

The same models on the responses not divided by time, with the climate change between the two ends
in place of its rate, give a different picture. The lag of a lake-period went with neither climate
change (`r f(slope('lag', 'climate_change'))` CCA distance per standardized unit of climate change)
nor fire (`r f(slope('lag', 'fire_activity'))`), and neither did the pace effect. The direction effect
went with both: lake-periods with more climate change (`r f(slope('direction_effect_total', 'climate_change'))`)
and more fire (`r f(slope('direction_effect_total', 'fire_activity'))`) ended with directions further
from the predicted one. The lag-rate and pace associations with the climate change rate therefore
rest on the division by time, while the direction association with fire holds in both forms. In the
Anthropocene, burned plots had a smaller total pace effect than unburned ones
(`r x = coefficients |> filter(metric == 'pace_effect_total', era == 'Anthropocene', term == 'burnedBurned'); f(x)`).
Fire activity stays a frequency in both forms, because a count of events would grow with the length
of the lake-period.

```{r fig-6-main}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_climate_fire_associations.pdf')
perf6 = read_output('community_predictor_models/model_performance.csv')
R2 = function(r, e) sprintf('%.2f', perf6$R2[perf6$response == r & perf6$era == e])
```

**Figure 6. Climate and fire associations.** Model slopes with conditional 95% confidence
intervals for the lag (black), the pace effect (pink) and the direction effect (blue), side by side
for each term, in the colours of Figure 1. Faded estimates have intervals that include zero. Top row
(A, B): the responses per century, the change in mismatch or the reduction in final mismatch under the
pace or direction correction divided by the elapsed time. Bottom row (C, D): the same responses not
divided by time. The panels of a row share one x scale. (A, C) Holocene lake-periods, model response
~ site + climate + fire activity with an AR(1) correlation within each lake and weights for the
number of samples at each end, where climate is the climate change rate in A and the climate change
between the two ends in C: `r perf6$n_MORA[perf6$response == 'lag_rate' & perf6$era == 'Holocene']` MORA and
`r perf6$n_NOCA[perf6$response == 'lag_rate' & perf6$era == 'Holocene']` NOCA lake-periods for the lag, and
`r perf6$n_MORA[perf6$response == 'pace_effect' & perf6$era == 'Holocene']` and `r perf6$n_NOCA[perf6$response == 'pace_effect' & perf6$era == 'Holocene']`
for pace and direction. The climate slope is per standardized unit of climate change per century (A)
or per standardized unit of climate change (C), and the fire slope per accepted event per century per
covered core. (B, D) Anthropocene plot pairs, model response ~ site + burned with park-specific
variances: `r perf6$n[perf6$response == 'lag_rate' & perf6$era == 'Anthropocene']` plot pairs for the lag
and `r perf6$n[perf6$response == 'pace_effect' & perf6$era == 'Anthropocene']` for pace and direction.
Descriptive R² is given below each panel. `r both_spans` Effects are in CCA distance per century (A, B)
or CCA distance (C, D) per unit of the term.

# Step 5a. Holocene against Anthropocene

**What and why.** Each response is compared between the Holocene stability periods, the
Holocene climate-change periods and the Anthropocene, within each park. The two Holocene types
are never pooled, so back-and-forth change in the stability periods cannot cancel the directional
change of the climate-change periods, and the parks are never pooled. The Holocene rows are the
lake-periods and the Anthropocene rows are the plot pairs, in one model per response with
group-specific residual spread, the endpoint weights and the AR(1) within each lake. Fire stays
out of these models, because it is measured differently in the two eras. Rates over a few decades
and over centuries are not on equal footing, since longer windows give lower rates, and every
comparison states both time spans. The three contrasts between period types in each park are tested
together for both parks, so each response has six contrasts, and their p-values are Holm-adjusted
within that family. Significance is read from the adjusted p-values. The intervals are the unadjusted
95% intervals.

**How it is calculated.**

```{r step5a-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/13_era_models.R', 'era-model')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/13_era_models.R', 'joint-correction-model')
```

**Result.**

```{r step5a-results}
era_dir = 'era_comparison'
means = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_means.csv'))
contrasts = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_contrasts.csv'))
folds = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_folds.csv'))
durations = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_durations.csv'))
response_label = c(climate_rate = 'Climate change rate', climate_change = 'Climate change (not divided by time)',
  pace_effect_total = 'Pace effect (not divided by time)', direction_effect_total = 'Direction effect (not divided by time)',
  turnover_rate = 'Turnover rate',
  displacement = 'Displacement (turnover, not divided by time)', lag_rate = 'Lag rate', lag = 'Lag',
  pace_effect = 'Pace effect', direction_effect = 'Direction effect')
span = function(type) { d = durations[durations$period_type == type, ]; sprintf('%g to %g', min(d$duration_min), max(d$duration_max)) }
spans = sprintf(paste('Holocene-C lake-periods span %s years, Holocene-S lake-periods %s years, and the',
  'Anthropocene plot pairs %s years.'), span('Holocene-C'), span('Holocene-S'), span('Anthropocene'))
means |> transmute(Response = response_label[response], Park = site, `Period type` = period_type, n,
    `Fitted mean` = estimate, `95% CI` = sprintf('%.3f to %.3f', conf_low, conf_high)) |>
  show_table('step5a_era_means', caption = paste('**Fitted means by period type and park.** Climate change',
    'rate in calibration SD per century, the climate change in calibration SD, the displacement, the lag and the',
    'effect totals in CCA distance, the other responses in CCA distance per century.', spans))
contrasts |> transmute(Response = response_label[response], Park = site, Contrast = contrast,
    Estimate = estimate, `95% CI` = sprintf('%.3f to %.3f', conf_low, conf_high), p = p_value,
    `p (Holm)` = p_adjusted) |>
  show_table('step5a_era_contrasts', caption = paste('**Contrasts between period types within each park**,',
    'with conditional 95% confidence intervals (unadjusted). p (Holm) is adjusted across the six contrasts of',
    'each response, three per park.', spans))
folds |> transmute(Response = response_label[response], Park = site, `Anthropocene over` = against,
    Fold = fold, `Quoted as speed` = ifelse(quoted_as_speed, 'yes', 'no')) |>
  show_table('step5a_era_folds', caption = paste('**Folds**: the Anthropocene fitted mean divided by the',
    'Holocene fitted mean of each type.', spans))
fold = function(r, p, a) folds$fold[folds$response == r & folds$site == p & folds$against == a]
holm_p = function(p) ifelse(p < .001, 'Holm p < 0.001', sprintf('Holm p = %.3f', p))
ct = function(r, p, k) { x = contrasts[contrasts$response == r & contrasts$site == p & contrasts$contrast == k, ]
  sprintf('%+.2f (%.2f to %.2f, %s)', x$estimate, x$conf_low, x$conf_high, holm_p(x$p_adjusted)) }
```

Climate changed `r sprintf('%.0f', fold('climate_rate', 'MORA', 'Holocene-C'))` times faster at MORA
and `r sprintf('%.0f', fold('climate_rate', 'NOCA', 'Holocene-C'))` times faster at NOCA in the
Anthropocene than in the Holocene climate-change periods. The forest turned over
`r sprintf('%.0f', fold('turnover_rate', 'MORA', 'Holocene-C'))` times faster at MORA and
`r sprintf('%.0f', fold('turnover_rate', 'NOCA', 'Holocene-C'))` times faster at NOCA. At MORA the lag
grew in the Anthropocene and did not grow in either Holocene type (Anthropocene minus Holocene-C
`r ct('lag_rate', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')`, minus Holocene-S
`r ct('lag_rate', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S')` CCA distance per century). At NOCA the lag
rate did not differ between the period types (`r ct('lag_rate', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')`
against Holocene-C). Within the Holocene, the C and S lake-periods did not differ in lag, pace or
direction in either park. `r spans`

Not divided by time, the climate still shifted further in the few decades of the Anthropocene than
over a whole Holocene lake-period (Anthropocene minus Holocene-C
`r ct('climate_change', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')` calibration SD at MORA,
`r ct('climate_change', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')` at NOCA). The distance the community moved
(the displacement) tells a different story
from its rate. At MORA the plots moved more in a few decades than the communities of the Holocene
climate-change periods did in centuries (Anthropocene minus Holocene-C
`r ct('displacement', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')` CCA distance), and as much as those of the
stability periods (`r ct('displacement', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S')`). At NOCA the plots moved
more than in the stability periods (`r ct('displacement', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S')`), while
their difference from the climate-change periods is not significant after the adjustment
(`r ct('displacement', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')`).
The pace and direction effects lose their era differences when they are not divided by time. At
MORA, the per-century pace effect of the Anthropocene exceeds that of both Holocene types
(`r ct('pace_effect', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')` against Holocene-C), and so does the
per-century direction effect (`r ct('direction_effect', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')`). As
totals, no contrast between the Anthropocene and a Holocene period type is significant after the
adjustment in either park (for example MORA direction against Holocene-S
`r ct('direction_effect_total', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S')`, NOCA pace against Holocene-C
`r ct('pace_effect_total', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')`). At NOCA the per-century pace and
direction effects do not differ between the eras either (pace against Holocene-C
`r ct('pace_effect', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')`). The Anthropocene effects are large per
century mainly because they build up over a few decades.

**Check: displacement and lag by lake-period duration.** Displacement and lag are totals, so a
longer lake-period could show more of both only because it is longer. The table gives their plain
means (no model) for the three duration classes the lake-periods fall into.

```{r step5a-duration-classes}
dc = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_duration_classes.csv'))
dc |> transmute(Park = site, Duration = duration_class, `Lake-periods` = lake_periods,
    `Stability / climate-change` = sprintf('%d / %d', stability, climate_change),
    Years = sprintf('%g to %g', duration_min, duration_max), `Mean displacement` = mean_displacement,
    `Mean absolute lag` = mean_absolute_lag, `Mean lag` = mean_lag) |>
  show_table('step5a_duration_classes', caption = paste('**Displacement and lag of the lake-periods by duration.**',
    'Plain means over the Holocene lake-periods of each park and duration class. The displacement is the distance',
    'the community moved in CCA space from the first to the last sampled century. The absolute lag is the size of',
    'the change in mismatch, |M at t2 minus M at t1|, and the lag is the same change with its sign. All three are',
    'in CCA distance and not divided by time.'))
dd = function(p, k, v) dc[[v]][dc$site == p & dc$duration_class == k]
```

At MORA the three longest lake-periods (over 2,000 years) moved further than the shorter ones
(mean displacement `r sprintf('%.3f', dd('MORA', 'over 2,000 years', 'mean_displacement'))` against
`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('MORA', '200 to 400 years', 'mean_displacement'))` for 200 to 400 years and
`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('MORA', '500 to 900 years', 'mean_displacement'))` for 500 to 900 years). At NOCA
the displacement did not grow with duration (`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('NOCA', '200 to 400 years', 'mean_displacement'))`,
`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('NOCA', '500 to 900 years', 'mean_displacement'))` and
`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('NOCA', 'over 2,000 years', 'mean_displacement'))`, the last from a single
lake-period). The absolute lag ranged from `r sprintf('%.3f', min(dc$mean_absolute_lag[dc$site == 'MORA']))` to
`r sprintf('%.3f', max(dc$mean_absolute_lag[dc$site == 'MORA']))` at MORA and from
`r sprintf('%.3f', min(dc$mean_absolute_lag[dc$site == 'NOCA']))` to
`r sprintf('%.3f', max(dc$mean_absolute_lag[dc$site == 'NOCA']))` at NOCA across the classes. The displacement
is the net movement from the first to the last century, so movement back and forth within a lake-period
does not add to it, and it does not grow in proportion to time. The rates of the long lake-periods are
low partly for that reason.

**Check: sensitivity to the paleoclimate bias correction.** The primary run uses the raw
CHELSA-TraCE21k paleoclimate. Its modern slice differs from the CHELSA V2.1 climate the CCA is
calibrated on, by a fixed offset per lake and month for temperature and a fixed ratio for
precipitation. [`R/sensitivity_bias_corrected.R`](R/sensitivity_bias_corrected.R) reruns stages 07 to
15 with that difference removed (`PALEO_USE_BIAS_CORRECTED = TRUE`) into `output_bias_corrected/`,
and leaves the primary outputs untouched. The climate periods are defined on the raw series in both
runs, so the same lake-periods are compared. Only the climate-predicted Holocene positions change.
The observed positions and the Anthropocene do not.

```{r step5a-bias-correction}

if (file.exists(file.path(bias_dir, 'sign_counts.csv'))) {

  bc |> transmute(Response = c(lag = 'Lag', pace_effect = 'Pace effect', direction_effect = 'Direction effect')[response],
      Park = site, `Lake-periods` = lake_periods, `Defined in both runs` = defined_in_both,
      `Keep their sign` = keep_sign, `Change sign` = change_sign) |>
    show_table('bias_correction_sign_counts', caption = paste('**Lake-periods that keep their sign when the',
      'paleoclimate is bias-corrected.** A pace or direction effect is undefined where a position did not move.'))
  readr::read_csv(file.path(bias_dir, 'lake_periods_raw_vs_corrected.csv'), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    show_table('bias_correction_lake_periods', caption = paste('**Lag, pace effect and direction effect of every',
      'lake-period, raw and bias-corrected paleoclimate side by side.** Lag in CCA distance, pace and direction',
      'effects in CCA distance per century.'))
  era_runs = function(path) readr::read_csv(file.path(path, '13_era_models', 'era_comparison', 'era_contrasts.csv'),
    show_col_types = FALSE) |> filter(response %in% c('lag', 'lag_rate', 'pace_effect', 'direction_effect'),
    contrast != 'Holocene-C - Holocene-S')
  bc_era = inner_join(era_runs(here::here('output')), era_runs(here::here('output_bias_corrected')),
    by = c('response', 'site', 'contrast'), suffix = c('_raw', '_corrected'))

      `Raw` = sprintf('%+.3f (%.3f to %.3f), %s', estimate_raw, conf_low_raw, conf_high_raw, holm_p(p_adjusted_raw)),
      `Bias-corrected` = sprintf('%+.3f (%.3f to %.3f), %s', estimate_corrected, conf_low_corrected,
        conf_high_corrected, holm_p(p_adjusted_corrected))) |>
    show_table('bias_correction_era_contrasts', caption = paste('**Era contrasts with the raw and the',

      'The Anthropocene values are the same in both runs.'))
} else cat('Run Rscript R/sensitivity_bias_corrected.R to fill this check.\n')
```

```{r step5a-bias-correction-text, results = 'asis'}
  k = function(r, p) bc[bc$response == r & bc$site == p, ]
  kk = function(r, p) sprintf('%d of %d', k(r, p)$keep_sign, k(r, p)$defined_in_both)
  e = function(r, p, c, run) { x = bc_era[bc_era$response == r & bc_era$site == p & bc_era$contrast == c, ]
    sprintf('%+.3f (%s)', x[[paste0('estimate_', run)]], holm_p(x[[paste0('p_adjusted_', run)]])) }
  cat(paste0('The result is poor at MORA. There the lag kept its sign in ', kk('lag', 'MORA'),

    kk('direction_effect', 'MORA'), '. At NOCA the lag kept its sign in ', kk('lag', 'NOCA'), ', the pace effect in ',
    kk('pace_effect', 'NOCA'), ' and the direction effect in ', kk('direction_effect', 'NOCA'), '. ',
    'The correction shifts the spring temperature of each lake by a fixed offset and scales its summer ',
    'precipitation by a fixed ratio, so it moves the climate-predicted positions of a lake together and changes ',
    'the mismatch at both ends of a lake-period. Most MORA Holocene lags and pace effects are small, and a small ',
    'change in the two mismatches is enough to flip their sign. The Holocene values of each lake-period are ',
    'therefore not robust at MORA. The era comparisons are more robust, because the Anthropocene values are far ',
    'from the Holocene ones: the MORA lag rate, Anthropocene minus Holocene-C, is ', e('lag_rate', 'MORA',
    'Anthropocene - Holocene-C', 'raw'), ' raw and ', e('lag_rate', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C', 'corrected'),
    ' corrected. The MORA lag contrasts change their meaning: against Holocene-C the lag goes from ',
    e('lag', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C', 'raw'), ' to ', e('lag', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C',
    'corrected'), ', and against Holocene-S from ', e('lag', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S', 'raw'), ' to ',
    e('lag', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S', 'corrected'), ', the latter because the long MORA S4 lake-periods ',
    'turn from positive to negative lags. Whether the MORA Anthropocene lag, not divided by time, exceeds the ',
    'Holocene one therefore depends on the paleoclimate correction. The NOCA pace contrast against ',
    'Holocene-C is ', e('pace_effect', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C', 'raw'), ' raw and ',
    e('pace_effect', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C', 'corrected'), ' corrected.\n'))
}
```

# Step 6. Species

**What and why.** The observed movement of a community between t1 and t2 is the sum of one
vector per species: the change in the species' share times the species' fixed position in the
CCA plane. Projecting each species' vector on a reference direction says how much that species
moved the community along it. Two measures are used, both per century. Along the direction the
prediction moved (`contrib_climate`), a positive value means the species carried the community with
the climate. The second measure, `contrib_lag`, splits the lag rate itself. The mismatch g, from the
predicted to the observed position, is taken at both ends (g1 at t1, g2 at t2), and m is their sum
divided by the sum of their lengths. Each species' vector projected on m is that species' part of the
lag rate, and the predicted movement projected on m, with its sign reversed, is the climate's part.
Because the change in mismatch, g2 − g1, is the observed movement minus the predicted movement, and
(g2 − g1)·m is exactly the change in the length of the mismatch, the species parts and the climate
part add up exactly to the lag rate (asserted). A negative species value means the species narrowed
the lag, a positive value that it widened it. Swapping the two surveys reverses every value, so the
measure has no direction of its own. It replaces `contrib_gap`, the projection on the mismatch at
the start alone. That measure leaned positive: a community sampled away from its predicted position
tends to come back towards it by chance, and run backwards in time it also appeared to close the
gap. `contrib_lag` is per century of the same interval as the lag rate.

**How it is calculated.**

```{r step6-code}
code_snippet('R/helpers/cca_transition_contributions.R', 'contrib-lag')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/15_contributions.R', 'species-means')
```

**Result.**

```{r step6-results}
species_means = read_output('species_contribution_models/species_means.csv')
species_means |> mutate(value = ifelse(interval_defined, sprintf('%+.3f (%.3f to %.3f)', estimate, conf_low, conf_high),
    ifelse(present, sprintf('%+.3f', estimate), 'absent'))) |>
  select(measure, species, site, period_type, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(measure, period_type), values_from = value) |>
  rename(Species = species, Park = site) |>
  show_table('step6_species_means', caption = paste('**Species contributions**, mean and 95% t-interval in CCA',
    'distance per century, per species, park and period type. Columns: measure (contrib_climate along the',
    'predicted movement, contrib_lag the species\' part of the lag rate) and period type. "absent": the species',
    'does not occur in that park and period type. contrib_lag includes the units where the community did not',
    'move (all species values zero), contrib_climate does not (epsilon rule).'))
lag_parts = read_output('cca_transition_contributions/lag_decomposition.csv')
tci = function(x) { n = length(x); m = mean(x); h = qt(.975, n - 1) * sd(x) / sqrt(n)
  sprintf('%+.3f (%+.3f to %+.3f)', m, m - h, m + h) }
lag_parts |> mutate(period_type = factor(period_type, levels = c('Holocene-S', 'Holocene-C', 'Anthropocene'))) |>
  group_by(Park = site, `Period type` = period_type) |>
  summarise(Units = n(), `Lag rate` = tci(lag_rate), `Species (sum)` = tci(species_sum),
    `Climate part` = tci(climate_part), .groups = 'drop') |>
  show_table('step6_lag_decomposition', caption = paste('**The lag rate split into the species and the climate.**',
    'Plain means over the lake-periods or plot pairs with 95% t-intervals, in CCA distance per century. In',
    'every unit the sum over species plus the climate part equals the lag rate. Positive values widen the lag.'))
```

The species vectors add up to the observed movement for every lake-period and plot pair (asserted).
```{r step6-numbers}
hol = species_means |> filter(period_type != 'Anthropocene')
hol_away = hol |> filter(interval_defined, conf_low > 0 | conf_high < 0)
lag_species = species_means |> filter(period_type == 'Anthropocene', measure == 'contrib_lag', interval_defined)
lp = lag_parts |> filter(era == 'Anthropocene') |> group_by(site) |>
  summarise(lag = mean(lag_rate), species = mean(species_sum), climate = mean(climate_part))
lpv = function(p, v) sprintf('%+.2f', lp[[v]][lp$site == p])
narrow = lag_species |> filter(conf_high < 0); widen = lag_species |> filter(conf_low > 0)
r_measures = species_means |> filter(period_type == 'Anthropocene') |>
  select(measure, species, site, estimate) |> pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = estimate) |>
  group_by(site) |> summarise(r = cor(contrib_climate, contrib_lag, use = 'complete.obs'))
```

In the Holocene every species mean is close to zero in both parks (largest absolute value
`r sprintf('%.3f', max(abs(hol$estimate)))` CCA distance per century).
`r nrow(hol_away)` of `r sum(hol$interval_defined)` Holocene intervals exclude zero
(`r paste(sprintf('%s, %s, %s, %s', hol_away$species, hol_away$site, hol_away$period_type, hol_away$measure), collapse = '; ')`),
all smaller than `r sprintf('%.3f', max(abs(hol_away$estimate)))` in absolute value. The Anthropocene
means are larger.

In the Anthropocene the climate's part of the lag rate is about the same in both parks
(`r lpv('MORA', 'climate')` at MORA, `r lpv('NOCA', 'climate')` at NOCA, CCA distance per century): the
predicted positions moved away from the communities. The parks differ in their species. At MORA the
species added to the lag (sum `r lpv('MORA', 'species')`), so the lag rate was `r lpv('MORA', 'lag')`. At
NOCA they narrowed it by more than the climate widened it (sum `r lpv('NOCA', 'species')`), so the lag
rate was `r lpv('NOCA', 'lag')`. Species whose interval lies below zero, which narrowed the lag:
`r paste(sprintf('%s (%s, %+.3f)', narrow$species, narrow$site, narrow$estimate), collapse = ', ')`.
Species whose interval lies above zero, which widened it:
`r paste(sprintf('%s (%s, %+.3f)', widen$species, widen$site, widen$estimate), collapse = ', ')`.
Across species the two measures are negatively correlated in the Anthropocene
(r = `r sprintf('%.2f', r_measures$r[r_measures$site == 'MORA'])` at MORA,
`r sprintf('%.2f', r_measures$r[r_measures$site == 'NOCA'])` at NOCA): species that moved the community with the
climate-predicted direction narrowed the lag, and those that moved it against that direction widened
it.

```{r step6-contrasts}
sc = read_output('species_contribution_models/species_contrasts.csv')
sc_sig = sc |> filter(p_adjusted < .05)
```

The period types of a species are compared with Welch tests, three contrasts per species, measure and
park, and the p-values are Holm-adjusted within each measure and park across all species and
contrasts. Of `r sum(!is.na(sc$p_value))` testable contrasts, `r sum(sc$p_value < .05, na.rm = TRUE)` have
p < 0.05 before the adjustment and `r nrow(sc_sig)` after it
(`r paste(sprintf('%s %s, %s, %s', sc_sig$species, sc_sig$site, sc_sig$contrast, sc_sig$measure), collapse = '; ')`).
`r if (nrow(sc_sig) && all(startsWith(sc_sig$contrast, 'Anthropocene'))) 'All of them set the Anthropocene against a Holocene period type.' else ''`

```{r fig-7-main}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_species_contributions.pdf')
```

**Figure 7. Species contributions in the Holocene and the Anthropocene.** Each species' vector is its
change in share between the first and the last sampled century of a lake-period, or between the
legacy survey and the resurvey of a plot, times its fixed position in the CCA plane. The upper row (following climate-predicted direction)
projects these vectors on the direction in which the climate-predicted position moved, and the lower
row (changing the climate-community lag) on the average direction of the mismatch at the two ends, so
that the species' values plus the climate's part add up to the lag rate. Labels at the top of each panel read with the row title: a species moved the community following or against the climate-predicted direction (upper row), and narrowed or widened the climate-community lag (lower row). The lower row includes the lake-periods and plot pairs whose composition did not change (all species values zero) and is per century of the same interval as the lag rate.
Species are ordered by the maximum elevation of the plots where they occur (the 605 plot pairs, both surveys, both parks), the highest at the top. Their names are shaded by that maximum in four grey steps, lightest below 1,500 m and black above 1,900 m (key below the figure). Names in bold are species absent from the Holocene record of both parks.
Symbols are means: triangles, Holocene stability periods, circles, Holocene climate-change periods,
diamonds, Anthropocene plot pairs (burned and unburned together). Large symbols with bars are means whose
95% t-interval excludes zero, small faded symbols are means whose interval includes zero. A species with no
Holocene symbols in a park is absent from that park's Holocene record.
Each park has its own x scale, symmetric around zero. `r both_spans` Contributions are in CCA distance per century.

Stages and helpers: [`R/pipeline/15_contributions.R`](R/pipeline/15_contributions.R),
[`R/helpers/cca_transition_contributions.R`](R/helpers/cca_transition_contributions.R),
[`R/figures/main_fig7_species.R`](R/figures/main_fig7_species.R).

# Numbers for the Results text

Every number below is read from an output of the run. Rates are per century. Intervals are 95%
conditional confidence intervals (models) or t-intervals (species). `r both_spans`

```{r numbers-setup}
f2 = function(x) sprintf('%+.3f', x)
ci = function(lo, hi) sprintf('%.3f to %.3f', lo, hi)
```

**Step 0, climate variables.**

```{r numbers-step0}
screening |> group_by(Set = set) |> summarise(`Max VIF` = max(VIF), `Adjusted R²` = first(adjusted_R2),
    `MORA lake-centuries outside (%)` = 100 * first(extrapolated_share_MORA),
    `NOCA lake-centuries outside (%)` = 100 * first(extrapolated_share_NOCA)) |>
  show_table('numbers_step0', caption = paste0('**Screening.** Adding MWT and WP to MSpT + SP: pseudo-F ',
    sprintf('%.2f', addback$pseudo_F[1]), ', p = ', sprintf('%.4f', addback$p_value[addback$design == 'Unrestricted']),
    ' unrestricted and ', sprintf('%.4f', addback$p_value[addback$design == 'Within parks']), ' within parks.'))
```

**Steps 1 to 4, periods and lake-periods.**

```{r numbers-units}
units |> group_by(Park = site, `Period type` = period_type) |>
  summarise(`Lake-periods` = n(), `Years (min)` = min(duration_yr), `Years (max)` = max(duration_yr),
    `Climate change rate (mean)` = mean(climate_rate), `Fire activity (min)` = min(fire_activity),
    `Fire activity (max)` = max(fire_activity), `Fire activity (mean)` = mean(fire_activity), .groups = 'drop') |>
  show_table('numbers_units', caption = sprintf(paste('**Lake-periods** (raw values, not model estimates). %d lake and',
    'period combinations had a sampled century, and %d had two or more.'), nrow(candidates), nrow(units)))
```

**Step 5a, era models: fitted means, contrasts and folds per park.**

```{r numbers-era}
means |> transmute(Response = response_label[response], Park = site, `Period type` = period_type, n,
    Mean = f2(estimate), `95% CI` = ci(conf_low, conf_high)) |>
  show_table('numbers_era_means', caption = '**Fitted means.**')
contrasts |> transmute(Response = response_label[response], Park = site, Contrast = contrast,
    Estimate = f2(estimate), `95% CI` = ci(conf_low, conf_high), p = p_value, `p (Holm)` = p_adjusted) |>
  show_table('numbers_era_contrasts', caption = paste('**Contrasts between period types.** p (Holm) is adjusted',
    'across the six contrasts of each response (three per park). Quote the adjusted p.'))
folds |> transmute(Response = response_label[response], Park = site, `Anthropocene over` = against, Fold = fold) |>
  show_table('numbers_era_folds', caption = '**Folds.** The Holocene-C fold is the one quoted as a speed.')
```

**Step 5, Holocene explanatory models and their Anthropocene counterpart.**

```{r numbers-step5}
coefficients |> filter(term != '(Intercept)') |>
  transmute(Response = label[metric], Era = era, Term = term, Estimate = f2(estimate),
    `95% CI` = ci(conf_low, conf_high), p = p_value) |>
  show_table('numbers_step5', caption = paste('**Slopes and contrasts.** Climate change rate: per standardized unit per',
    'century. Fire activity: per event per century per covered core. Each model has one group contrast (site, and',
    'burned minus unburned in the Anthropocene), so these p-values need no adjustment for multiple contrasts.'))
```

**Step 6, species.**

```{r numbers-step6}
species_means |> filter(interval_defined) |>
  group_by(Measure = measure, Park = site, `Period type` = period_type) |>
  summarise(Species = n(), `Interval above zero` = sum(conf_low > 0), `Interval below zero` = sum(conf_high < 0),
    `Largest absolute mean` = max(abs(estimate)), .groups = 'drop') |>
  show_table('numbers_step6', caption = '**Species means** per measure, park and period type (species with a defined interval).')
```

**Figure 2, climate rates.**

```{r numbers-fig2}
read_output('figures/holocene_climate_level_rates.csv') |>
  transmute(Kind = kind, Variable = variable, Period = coalesce(period, ''), `cal BP` = t, `Rate per century` = rate) |>
  bind_rows(rates2 |> transmute(Kind = 'Anthropocene plot median', Variable = variable, Period = site,
    `Rate per century` = rate)) |>
  show_table('numbers_fig2', caption = '**Real-unit climate rates per century** (°C for MSpT, mm for SP).')
```

```{r numbers-doubts}
      screening$adjusted_R2[screening$set == 'MSpT + SP'][1], screening$adjusted_R2[screening$set == 'All four'][1],
```

```{r fig-app-charcoal}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/fig_charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh.pdf')
cc = read_output('figures/charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh_correlations.csv')
cm = read_output('figures/charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh_event_matching.csv')
cr = function(rec, what) { x = cc[cc$record == rec & cc$against == what, ]; sprintf('%+.2f (p = %.2f)', x$rho, x$p_shift) }
acc = 'Walsh charcoal accumulation (mean of three cores)'; frq = 'Walsh fire frequency (mean of three cores)'
bench = cc[cc$against == 'Walsh core against core', ]
```

**Fig. A4. Charcoal of the Walsh et al. (2017) Sunrise Ridge cores against the charcoal of the MORA
vegetation lakes (Dunwiddie).** The MORA fire values of the analysis come from the three Sunrise Ridge
cores, while the vegetation records come from Jay Bath, Log Wallow and Reflection Pond. The upper three
rows show each Sunrise Ridge core's charcoal accumulation rate (grey) with its background (dashed) and
the fire events accepted by tapas (dark red triangles). The lower three rows show the charcoal fragments
counted in each Dunwiddie macrofossil sample. They are a concentration, since all samples of a core had
the same volume, and the samples above each lake's 75th percentile are filled. Every Walsh event is
carried as a faint line through all rows. Time runs from 7,000 cal BP to the present, the span of the
Dunwiddie records. The two kinds of record follow opposite long-term courses: the Sunrise Ridge cores
hold most of their charcoal and events in the last 3,500 years, while Jay Bath and Log Wallow hold most
of theirs before 4,000 cal BP. Correlated over `r unique(cc$bins)[1]` bins of 500 years with the mean of
the three cores (Spearman, p from circular shifts that keep each record's autocorrelation, so that the
smallest possible p is about 0.07), Jay Bath gives `r cr('Jay Bath', acc)` with the charcoal accumulation
and `r cr('Jay Bath', frq)` with the fire frequency, Log Wallow `r cr('Log Wallow', acc)` and
`r cr('Log Wallow', frq)`, and Reflection Pond `r cr('Reflection Pond', acc)` and
`r cr('Reflection Pond', frq)`. The Sunrise Ridge cores agree only weakly with one another
(`r paste(sprintf('%s %+.2f', bench$record, bench$rho), collapse = ', ')`). A Dunwiddie peak lies within
200 years of `r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$matched[cm$record == 'Jay Bath'])`%,
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$matched[cm$record == 'Log Wallow'])`% and
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$matched[cm$record == 'Reflection Pond'])`% of the `r cm$walsh_events[1]` Walsh
events at Jay Bath, Log Wallow and Reflection Pond, against
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$chance[cm$record == 'Jay Bath'])`%,
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$chance[cm$record == 'Log Wallow'])`% and
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$chance[cm$record == 'Reflection Pond'])`% expected by chance. The Sunrise Ridge
record therefore gives no evidence of the fire history at the vegetation lakes, and the MORA fire values
should be read as regional at best. The Dunwiddie values are concentrations, not accumulation rates, so
a change in sedimentation rate could shape part of their long-term course. Script:
[`R/figures/supp_charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh.R`](R/figures/supp_charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh.R).

**Figure 1. Conceptual framework (caption revisions).** The drawing is unchanged. In panel B, the lag
is the difference between the mismatches at t2 and t1, the first and last sampled century of a
lake-period (one lake within one climate period), and the lag rate is that difference per century.
In panel C, "at the same time point t" becomes "at t2". The axis labels may read "Spring temperature"
and "Summer precipitation".

# 1. Modern vegetation

Legacy surveys and resurveys of the same plots at Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades
(NOCA) National Parks were matched, cleaned and harmonized to one tree taxonomy
(`R/pipeline/01_clean_mora_vegetation.R`, `R/pipeline/02_clean_noca_vegetation.R`).

```{r fig-s1}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/stage_adult_seedling_past_present.pdf')
```

**Fig. S1. Tree species occurrence by developmental stage in legacy surveys and resurveys.**
Number of plots in which each species was recorded as an adult tree or seedling/regeneration at
Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades (NOCA) National Parks, following taxonomic harmonization
and exclusion of understory taxa, but before applying the CCA frequency threshold. Species could
occur in both vegetation stages within the same plot. At MORA, seedlings were defined as
individuals 10–140 cm tall at both survey dates. At NOCA, however, legacy surveys classified
individuals 0–3 m tall as regeneration and those taller than 3 m as adults, whereas resurveys
recorded seedlings of 10–140 cm and adults taller than 1.4 m. Consequently, differences between
vegetation stages at NOCA should be interpreted cautiously because size-class definitions
differed between surveys.

```{r fig-s2}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/plots_to_cca.pdf')
```

**Fig. S2. Selection of vegetation records for canonical correspondence analysis (CCA).**
Flowchart summarizing the matching, cleaning, and selection of legacy–resurvey plots (upper
panels) and Holocene macrofossil samples (lower panels) from Mount Rainier (MORA, blue) and North
Cascades (NOCA, orange) National Parks. The final set of eligible paired plots was used both to
calibrate the CCA using legacy community composition and to assess contemporary community
change, whereas Holocene samples were projected into the fitted ordination. Plots without any
retained tree species at either survey date were excluded because they could not be assigned an
observed CCA position. Sample sizes and reasons for exclusion are indicated at each step.

**Legacy plot area at NOCA.** Every resurvey plot is 500 m², but the NOCA legacy plots range
from 25 to 400 m². A small legacy plot can miss species that the resurvey then records, which would
show up as turnover. The table gives the NOCA plot pairs used in the analysis by legacy plot area, with their
richness and the Anthropocene responses of Step 5a. It is descriptive only.

```{r vegetation-noca-plot-area}
pa = read_output('report/noca_plot_area_responses.csv')
pci = function(m, lo, hi) ifelse(is.na(lo), sprintf('%.3f', m), sprintf('%.3f (%.3f to %.3f)', m, lo, hi))
pa |> transmute(`Legacy area (m²)` = legacy_area, Plots = plots,
    `Richness, legacy` = sprintf('%.2f', richness_legacy_mean), `Richness, resurvey` = sprintf('%.2f', richness_resurvey_mean),
    `Turnover rate` = pci(turnover_rate_mean, turnover_rate_low, turnover_rate_high),
    Lag = pci(lag_mean, lag_low, lag_high), `Lag rate` = pci(lag_rate_mean, lag_rate_low, lag_rate_high)) |>
  show_table('noca_plot_area_responses', caption = paste('**NOCA plot pairs by legacy plot area.** Richness is',
    'the mean number of the retained CCA taxa present in a plot. Turnover rate, lag and lag rate are plain means',
    'with 95% t-intervals (no model): the turnover and lag rates in CCA distance per century, the lag in CCA',
    'distance. The single 36 m² plot has no interval.'))
pa_row = function(a) pa[pa$legacy_area == a, ]
```

The smallest legacy plots did not record fewer of the CCA taxa: `r sprintf('%.2f', pa_row('25')$richness_legacy_mean)`
taxa per 25 m² plot against `r sprintf('%.2f', pa_row('100')$richness_legacy_mean)` per 100 m² plot. Their
turnover rate was not higher (`r sprintf('%.2f', pa_row('25')$turnover_rate_mean)` against
`r sprintf('%.2f', pa_row('100')$turnover_rate_mean)` CCA distance per century), and the intervals of the
three common areas overlap for every response. The NOCA Anthropocene results do not rest on the small
legacy plots.

`r details_link('01_vegetation_cleaning', 'Cleaning details')` (plot-by-plot decisions, NOCA tree
corrections, survey dates, raw-data provenance).

# 2. Climate

Modern climate is CHELSA V2.1 monthly climate in a survey-specific window for every plot
(`R/pipeline/04_modern_climate.R`); Holocene climate is CHELSA-TraCE21k at each lake and century
(`R/pipeline/07_paleo_climate.R`).

```{r fig-s3}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/test_survey_year_anomaly.pdf')
```

**Fig. S3. Climate conditions and survey-specific climate windows for the Anthropocene.** Upper
panels show annual climate variation from CHELSA v2.1 (1979–2021), averaged across the paired
vegetation plots at Mount Rainier (MORA, blue) and North Cascades (NOCA, orange) National Parks.
Variables include mean annual temperature (MAT), annual precipitation (AP), and the four seasonal
seasonal variables mean spring temperature (MSpT), mean winter temperature (MWT), summer
precipitation (SP), and winter precipitation (WP); MSpT and SP constrain the CCA. Shaded areas indicate the common legacy climate
window (1979–1989). Lower panels show the six-year climate windows used for each resurvey year
(Y−5 through Y), together with the number of paired plots (n) surveyed in that year. Winter
calculations also included December of the preceding calendar year. Climate conditions were
therefore calculated separately for each plot according to its resurvey year.

```{r fig-s4}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/climate_holocene_timeseries.pdf', page = 2)
```

**Fig. S4. Correlations among climate variables during the Holocene and Anthropocene.** Pearson
correlation coefficients (r) were calculated across lake locations and 100-year climate intervals
for the Holocene (CHELSA-TraCE21k, left) and across vegetation plots and survey periods for the
Anthropocene (CHELSA v2.1, right). Red indicates positive correlations and blue indicates negative
correlations, with numerical values showing Pearson's r. Climate variables include mean annual
(MAT), spring (MSpT), summer (MST), and winter (MWT) temperature, and annual (AP), spring (SpP),
summer (SP), and winter (WP) precipitation. Spring corresponds to March–May, summer to June–August,
and winter to December–February.

**Choice of CCA constraints.** Candidate variables are screened by their correlations (Fig. S4)
and by their variance inflation in the fitted CCA, keeping one temperature and one precipitation
variable. With the four seasonal variables MSpT, MWT, SP and WP, the two temperatures had variance
inflation factors near 30 and opposite-signed coefficients that are not identifiable. The CCA is
therefore constrained by spring temperature, the temperature that changes most through the
Holocene, and summer precipitation. Figures in the CCA plane are rotated rigidly by the varimax
angle so that the two arrows lie along the axes; distances and angles, and therefore every
tracking metric, are unchanged by the rotation (decision of 2026-11-09 in
`r details_link('10_decisions', 'Decisions')`). The constraints of this build:

```{r cca-vif}
read_output('cca_climate_contributions.csv') |>
  transmute(Variable = variable, Label = variable_label, VIF, `CCA1 score` = CCA1, `CCA2 score` = CCA2) |>
  show_table('cca_constraint_vif', digits = 2)
```

`r details_link('02_climate', 'Climate details')` (survey windows, TraCE21k against V2.1, full
correlation tables).

# Appendix S1. Construction of the Holocene age–depth models

### S1.1 Why an age–depth model was required

The macrofossils are measured at known depths in a sediment core, but depth itself does not
provide an age. Sediment does not necessarily accumulate at a constant rate: for example, 1 cm of
sediment can represent relatively few years during rapid accumulation and many more years during
slow accumulation. Chronological control is available only at selected depths, through
radiocarbon dates, dated volcanic deposits, ²¹⁰Pb dating, or other independently dated horizons.
We therefore required an age–depth model to estimate the calendar age of every depth between
these dated points and, importantly, to quantify uncertainty in those estimated ages.

We used the rbacon R package, which reconstructs sediment accumulation histories within a Bayesian
framework (Blaauw & Christen 2011). Rather than drawing a single line through the dated horizons,
Bacon estimates many age–depth histories that are compatible with the chronological evidence and
assumptions about sediment accumulation. The distribution of these histories represents the
posterior chronological uncertainty shown in Fig. S5.

### S1.2 Chronological controls and radiocarbon calibration

For each core, we assembled chronological controls for which both sediment depth and age
information were available (Table S1.1). For MORA, these consisted of the core surfaces, seven
radiocarbon dates from Jay Bath and Log Wallow, dated volcanic tephra horizons, and a basal
radiocarbon age for Reflection Pond. Reflection Pond contained no radiocarbon dates of its own and
was therefore constrained by the core surface, tephra horizons, and this basal control. For
Panther Potholes, we reproduced the chronology archived in the Neotoma database using the core
surface, five ²¹⁰Pb ages, six Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS) radiocarbon dates, and three
tephra horizons. We used the corrected control depths archived in Neotoma rather than the depths
reported in Prichard et al. (2009), which contain documented depth errors.

Radiocarbon ages are expressed in ¹⁴C years and cannot be treated directly as calendar ages
because atmospheric ¹⁴C concentrations have varied through time. We therefore supplied
radiocarbon ages and their laboratory errors as uncalibrated dates (cc = 1), which Bacon
calibrated against the IntCal20 Northern Hemisphere calibration curve (Reimer et al. 2020). This
converts each radiocarbon measurement into a probability distribution of plausible calendar ages.
Controls already expressed in calendar years, including the core surfaces and tephra ages, were
supplied directly (cc = 0) and were not calibrated.

The seven MORA radiocarbon ages and their laboratory errors were taken directly from Dunwiddie
(1986). For all other chronological controls, the source and interpretation of the assigned age
uncertainty are reported explicitly in Table S1.1. The Reflection Pond basal control is the mean
of the two basal radiocarbon ages of Jay Bath (QL-1704) and Log Wallow (QL-1728), 6015 ± 110 ¹⁴C yr
BP with the larger of the two laboratory errors, following P. Dunwiddie's advice that the three
basins share the same basal age (pers. comm.).

For Panther Potholes, the five ²¹⁰Pb ages were derived using a Constant Rate of Supply (CRS)
model. We retained the error values used in the archived Gavin chronology for the primary model;
however, these values correspond numerically to the ²¹⁰Pb activity uncertainties reported by
Prichard et al. (2009), rather than to independently estimated age uncertainties in years. We
therefore evaluated this uncertainty specification in a separate sensitivity analysis described
below.

```{r table-s1-1}
read_output('table_S1_1_chronological_controls.csv', col_types = readr::cols(.default = 'c')) |>
  show_table('table_S1_1_chronological_controls',
    caption = paste('**Table S1.1. Chronological controls used in the four Bayesian age–depth models.**',
      'For cc = 1, the entered age is an uncalibrated ¹⁴C age calibrated with IntCal20. For cc = 0,',
      'the entered age is already in calibrated years before present (cal yr BP; present = A.D. 1950).'))
```

### S1.3 Bayesian age–depth models

We fitted each core independently with Bacon using the settings summarized in Table S1.2. Bacon
divided each sediment core into 5-cm sections and estimated an accumulation time, in yr cm⁻¹, for
each section. Accumulation times were allowed to differ among sections but were correlated between
neighbouring sections through the model's memory parameter. The chronological controls in
Table S1.1 were then used to update these prior expectations and generate the posterior age–depth
chronology shown in Fig. S5.

The three MORA cores were modelled using the same accumulation and memory priors. Panther Potholes
instead retained the settings of the archived Bacon chronology in the Neotoma database so that our
model reproduced the published chronology while providing the complete posterior age–depth draws
required for subsequent analyses. All runs are seeded (seed 42).

```{r table-s1-2}
read_output('table_S1_2_rbacon_parameters.csv', col_types = readr::cols(.default = 'c')) |>
  show_table('table_S1_2_rbacon_parameters',
    caption = '**Table S1.2. rbacon parameters used to construct the age–depth models.**')
```

The thick volcanic deposits required one additional treatment. The MSH-Y tephra was represented as
an instantaneous depositional interval in all three MORA cores, including the 58-cm interval at Log
Wallow containing both primary and redeposited Y tephra. At Panther Potholes, the MSH-P, MSH-Y,
and Mazama tephra intervals were treated in the same way. Bacon therefore removed these intervals
while estimating gradual sediment accumulation and reinserted them without adding elapsed time.
These intervals are shown as vertical grey bands in Fig. S5.

```{r fig-s5}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/fig_bacon_agedepth_slump.pdf')
```

**Fig. S5. Bayesian age–depth models for the Jay Bath, Log Wallow, and Reflection Pond cores at
MORA and the Panther Potholes core at NOCA.** For each core, the three upper panels show, from left
to right, the Markov chain Monte Carlo trace, the prior (green) and posterior (grey) distributions
of sediment accumulation time, and the prior and posterior distributions of memory. In the main
panels, depth increases along the x-axis and age is expressed as calibrated years before present.
Coloured distributions at dated depths represent the chronological controls and their
uncertainty. The grey field represents the posterior distribution of possible age–depth
relationships; the central red line shows the posterior age–depth estimate and the outer dotted
lines the 95% posterior interval. Vertical grey bands identify tephra intervals treated as
instantaneous deposition.

For Panther Potholes, we reproduced the archived Neotoma chronology as the primary model. However,
Prichard et al. (2009) report uncertainties for measured ²¹⁰Pb activity, in DPM g⁻¹, and the same
numerical values were entered as age errors, in years, in the archived chronology. We therefore
fitted a sensitivity model in which the five ²¹⁰Pb controls were each assigned an assumed ±10-year
age error, all other controls and settings unchanged (Fig. S6).

```{r fig-s6}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/fig_bacon_pb210_sensitivity.pdf')
```

**Fig. S6. Sensitivity of the Panther Potholes age–depth chronology to uncertainty assigned to the
five ²¹⁰Pb controls in the upper 35 cm of the core.** The left panel shows that the two posterior
chronologies are nearly identical below the ²¹⁰Pb-dated section, whereas the right panel shows the
expected increase in uncertainty within the upper 35–40 cm. The uncertainty assigned to the ²¹⁰Pb
controls affects the precision of the most recent chronology but does not materially alter the
deeper Holocene chronology used in our analyses.

`r details_link('03_chronology', 'Chronology details')` (every control and its source).

# Appendix S2. Reconstruction and classification of fire histories

### S2.1 Holocene charcoal records

For MORA, we reconstructed Holocene fire activity using the Sunrise Lake, Shadow Lake, and Little
Sunrise Lake macrocharcoal records from Walsh et al. (2017). These records provide evidence of
regional fire activity on Sunrise Ridge and are independent of the Jay Bath, Log Wallow, and
Reflection Pond records used to reconstruct vegetation. For NOCA, we reconstructed Holocene fire
activity using the Panther Potholes macrocharcoal record of Prichard et al. (2009), extracted from
the archived Neotoma record and dated with the Panther Potholes chronology of Appendix S1. Thus,
at NOCA fire and vegetation records share the same core and chronology.

### S2.2 Identification of individual fire events

We reconstructed the fire-event detection analyses of Walsh et al. (2017) and Prichard et al.
(2009) within a common workflow implemented with the R package tapas
(`R/pipeline/08_fire_records.R`). CHAR was interpolated to regular intervals, its slowly varying
background estimated by robust LOWESS, and candidate fire events identified where the residual
peak component exceeded a record-specific threshold of the background noise. Candidates were
screened with a 75-year minimum-count test (p ≤ 0.05), and consecutive exceedances were treated as
one event. Record-specific settings are given in Table S2.1.

```{r table-s2-1}
events = read_output('holocene_fire_source_events.csv') |> count(lake, name = 'Accepted fire events')
read_output('holocene_fire_source_settings.csv') |>
  left_join(events, by = 'lake') |>
  transmute(Site = site, `Fire record` = if_else(lake == 'PantherPotholes', 'Panther Potholes', lake),
    `Interpolation interval (years)` = interpolation_years,
    `Background window (years)` = smoothing_years,
    `Peak threshold` = paste0(100 * threshold_probability, '%'), `Accepted fire events`) |>
  show_table('table_S2_1_fire_detection_parameters',
    caption = paste('**Table S2.1. Parameters used to reconstruct individual Holocene fire events.**',
      'All records were also screened with the same 75-year minimum-count test (p ≤ 0.05).',
      'MORA settings follow Walsh et al. (2017) and Panther Potholes settings Prichard et al. (2009),',
      'except its 12-year interpolation interval, the median resolution of our updated chronology.'))
```

```{r fig-s7}
show_figure('report/figures/worked_examples/fig_fire_event_detection_workflow.pdf', page = 2)
```

**Fig. S7. Identification of Holocene fire events in the four records.** The residual peak
component is the difference between interpolated charcoal accumulation rates (CHAR) and the
background estimated with the record's robust LOWESS window. Candidate events exceed the local
noise threshold (dashed line) and are then screened with a 75-year minimum-count test
(p ≤ 0.05): filled circles are accepted events, red crosses rejected candidates. The manuscript
example is Little Sunrise Lake (lower left; 500-year background, 95th percentile).

### S2.3 Identification of high-fire periods

We calculated fire-event frequency within centered 1,000-year windows evaluated every 100 years,
normalized each record by its own maximum, averaged the normalized MORA records wherever at least
two were available, and identified high-fire periods separately for each site with

**High-fire threshold = median + 1.4826 × MAD (Eq. 1)**

where MAD is the median absolute deviation of the normalized site-level fire-frequency series.
Consecutive above-threshold dates form one high-fire period; gaps are not bridged and no minimum
duration is imposed (`R/pipeline/11_climate_eras_high_fire.R`; worked example in
`r details_link('09_worked_examples', 'Worked examples')`).

```{r high-fire-periods}
read_output('holocene_era_high_fire_periods.csv') |>
  transmute(Site = site, `Older (cal BP)` = older_cal_bp, `Younger (cal BP)` = younger_cal_bp,
    `Duration (years)` = duration_years, `Maximum normalized frequency` = maximum_normalized_frequency,
    Threshold = threshold) |>
  show_table('high_fire_periods', digits = 2, caption = '**High-fire periods identified by Eq. 1.**')
```

### S2.4 Reproducibility against the original studies

We compared the number of events identified by tapas with those reported by Walsh et al. (2017)
and Prichard et al. (2009), and additionally reproduced the MORA analyses with CharAnalysis R
2.0.3 (Table S2.2). Event counts differed from the published values, including with CharAnalysis,
suggesting that discrepancies arise partly from differences between software implementations. We
retained tapas for one consistent detection procedure across all four records, preserving their
source-specific settings rather than tuning parameters to reproduce published counts.

```{r table-s2-2}
# Published Panther Potholes total: Prichard et al. (2009), as in the Supporting Information draft.
PRICHARD_2009_PUBLISHED_EVENTS = 59L
mora = read_output('walsh_charanalysis_software_comparison.csv') |>
  transmute(Site = 'MORA', Lake = sub(' Lake$', '', lake), Published = published_total_episodes,
    `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = official_r_episodes, tapas = tapas_episodes)
noca = tibble(Site = 'NOCA', Lake = 'Panther Potholes', Published = PRICHARD_2009_PUBLISHED_EVENTS,
  `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = NA_real_, tapas = events$`Accepted fire events`[events$lake == 'PantherPotholes'])
difference = function(t, p) sprintf('%+d (%+.0f%%)', as.integer(t - p), 100 * (t - p) / p)
rows = bind_rows(
  mora |> arrange(match(Lake, c('Sunrise', 'Shadow', 'Little Sunrise'))),
  mora |> summarise(Site = 'MORA total', Lake = '', across(c(Published, `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3`, tapas), sum)),
  noca,
  bind_rows(mora, noca) |> summarise(Site = 'Both sites', Lake = '', Published = sum(Published),
    `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = NA_real_, tapas = sum(tapas))) |>
  mutate(`Difference from published` = difference(tapas, Published))
show_table(rows, 'table_S2_2_fire_event_counts', digits = 0,
  caption = paste('**Table S2.2. Holocene fire-event counts reported in the original studies and',
    'reconstructed with CharAnalysis R 2.0.3 (MORA only) and tapas (all four records).**'))
```

# 4. Canonical correspondence analysis

One CCA is fitted to the legacy composition of the `r cca_value('calibration_plots')` matched
plots (MORA and NOCA pooled), constrained by the climate variables above (scaling 1, Hill = FALSE).
Resurvey plots and Holocene samples are projected into it: their climate gives a predicted (LC)
position and their composition an observed (WA) position.

```{r cca-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/10_cca.R', 'cca-fit')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/10_cca.R', 'cca-projection')
```

```{r cca-axes}
read_output('cca_axes.csv') |>
  transmute(Axis = axis, Eigenvalue = eigenvalue, `% total inertia` = percent_total_inertia,
    `% constrained inertia` = percent_constrained_inertia) |>
  show_table('cca_axes', caption = sprintf('**CCA axes.** Constrained inertia: %.1f%% of the total.',
    as.numeric(cca_value('constrained_percent'))))
read_output('cca_anova.csv') |>
  transmute(Test = test, Component = component, df, `Pseudo-F` = pseudo_F,
    `p (unrestricted)` = p_unrestricted, `p (within parks)` = p_within_parks) |>
  show_table('cca_permutation_tests', caption = paste('**Permutation tests** (9,999 permutations,',
    'unrestricted and restricted within parks).'))
```
